paths/how-the-denominations-multiplied/s: From one Church confessing one faith to tens of thousands of denominations: a guided tour of the great divisions, from the 5th-century Christological schisms and the East-West split to the Reformation, dissent, revival, Pentecostalism and the Global South, and of the movements that have tried to reunite Christians.
Fault lines in the ancient Church

The first lasting divisions were over Christ, not church order. After the Council of Ephesus (431) the Church of the East, mostly in the Persian Empire, did not accept its condemnation of Nestorius; after Chalcedon (451) the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian churches rejected the "two natures" formula and became the Oriental Orthodox family. Language, empire and politics deepened theological disagreements that recent dialogues suggest were partly verbal.
East and West drift apart

Greek East and Latin West grew apart over centuries: papal authority, the filioque, leavened or unleavened bread and clerical celibacy. The mutual excommunications of 1054 are a symbolic date; the sack of Constantinople by crusaders in 1204 made the break felt at popular level. Eastern Catholic churches later united with Rome while keeping Eastern rites (e.g. the Union of Brest, 1596).
Medieval dissent: Waldensians and Hussites

Reform movements that stressed poverty, preaching and Scripture in the vernacular were pushed out of the medieval Church. Waldo’s Poor of Lyon (1170s) survived persecution in the Alps; Jan Hus was burned at Constance in 1415 and his followers formed Hussite churches, from which the Moravian Unity of Brethren descends.
Luther and the evangelical churches

Martin Luther’s protest of 1517 over indulgences became a dispute about grace, Scripture and authority. Princes and cities that accepted the Augsburg Confession (1530) formed territorial Lutheran churches, legally recognised in the Empire by the Peace of Augsburg (1555) on the principle that the ruler decides the region’s religion.
Reformed, radical and Anglican

The Reformers soon divided among themselves. Zwingli and Luther failed to agree on the Lord’s Supper at Marburg (1529); Calvin’s Geneva shaped the Reformed and Presbyterian churches; Anabaptists began believers’ baptism in Zurich in 1525 and were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike; England’s break with Rome (1534) created the Church of England, a church both catholic and reformed in its own self-understanding.
Church order divides Protestants

Should a church be governed by bishops, by elders in presbyteries, or by each congregation? English Puritans split over this question into Presbyterians and Congregationalists (Independents); the Westminster Assembly (1643) produced Presbyterian standards. Anabaptist groups also subdivided into Mennonites, Hutterites and, in 1693, the Amish.
Dissenters: Baptists and Quakers

English exiles under John Smyth in Amsterdam (1609) baptised believers only and became the first Baptists; George Fox’s Quakers (1652) rejected outward sacraments and clergy for the inward light. The Great Ejection of 1662 pushed some 2,000 Puritan ministers out of the Church of England; the Toleration Act of 1689 accepted Dissent as a permanent feature of English religion.
Revival makes new churches

Evangelical revival produced new denominations. Wesley’s Methodists separated from the Church of England after his death; American revivals spawned the Stone-Campbell Restoration movement, the African Methodist Episcopal Church (1816), Holiness churches and the Salvation Army. Prophetic movements arose from the same milieu: Seventh-day Adventists after the Millerite Great Disappointment (1844), and outside historic Nicene orthodoxy the Latter-day Saints (1830) and Jehovah’s Witnesses (1879).
Pentecostalism and the Global South

The Azusa Street revival (1906) launched Pentecostalism, which itself divided: Assemblies of God (1914), Oneness Pentecostals (1913-16) and countless independent churches. In Africa, prophets such as William Wade Harris and Simon Kimbangu inspired African-initiated churches; in China, house churches grew outside state control after 1949. Most new denominations are now founded in the Global South.
Counter-current: the search for unity

Alongside division runs reunion. The Edinburgh Missionary Conference (1910) launched the modern ecumenical movement; the Church of South India (1947) joined Anglicans, Methodists and Reformed; the World Council of Churches (1948) and Vatican II’s decree on ecumenism (1964) changed relations between churches. Critics still debate whether visible unity or spiritual unity is the goal.
paths/how-the-denominations-multiplied/q: Which churches separated after the Council of Chalcedon (451)?
The Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian)
Churches that rejected Chalcedon’s "in two natures" formula became the Oriental Orthodox family; the Church of the East had separated after Ephesus (431).
What is the symbolic date usually given for the split between Eastern Orthodox and Catholics?
Mutual excommunications in 1054 are the symbolic date, though the estrangement developed over centuries and hardened after 1204.
Where did the first adult (believers’) baptisms of the Anabaptist movement take place in 1525?
Conrad Grebel and others baptised each other in Zurich in January 1525.
What issue chiefly divided Presbyterians and Congregationalists?
Both were Reformed in doctrine; they disagreed over whether congregations are governed by presbyteries or are self-governing.
Who led the English exiles who formed the first Baptist church in Amsterdam (1609)?
John Smyth and Thomas Helwys led the first General Baptists in Amsterdam.
Which movement grew from the Millerite "Great Disappointment" of 1844?
Adventists reinterpreted the failed prediction and organised as the Seventh-day Adventist Church in 1863.
Which 1910 event is often seen as the start of the modern ecumenical movement?
The Edinburgh conference led to the International Missionary Council and eventually the World Council of Churches (1948).
paths/the-great-schools-of-theology/summ: How have Christians thought about God? A tour of the great theological schools and methods, from Alexandria and Antioch through monks and scholastics, Reformation orthodoxy and Pietism, Enlightenment and liberalism, Barth and the 20th-century revivals, to the liberation, contextual and Pentecostal theologies of world Christianity.
paths/the-great-schools-of-theology/step: Alexandria and Antioch: how to read the Bible

Clement and Origen in Alexandria used philosophy and sought spiritual senses beneath the letter; Diodore, Theodore of Mopsuestia and Chrysostom in Antioch insisted on history and grammar. Their debate about allegory and the literal sense still shapes biblical interpretation, and the Church of the East kept Theodore as "the Interpreter" at Nisibis.
Believe in order to understand

Tertullian asked what Athens had to do with Jerusalem, but Augustine taught the West that faith opens the way to understanding. Anselm made "faith seeking understanding" the programme of his Proslogion (1078), at the hinge between monastic and scholastic theology.
Cloister and school

Bernard of Clairvaux practised theology as prayerful savouring of Scripture; Abelard and Peter Lombard posed questions and resolved authorities by logic. Bernard secured Abelard’s condemnation in 1141, but Lombard’s Sentences became the textbook of the universities.
Aquinas, Scotus and Ockham

Thomas Aquinas built a synthesis of Aristotle and revelation in which grace perfects nature; after the Paris condemnations of 1277, Duns Scotus stressed God’s freedom and William of Ockham’s via moderna limited what reason can prove. Luther was trained in Ockham’s school.
Back to the sources and the Reformation

Humanists such as Erasmus called theology back to the original languages; Luther attacked scholastic theology itself. Within a generation Lutheran and Reformed orthodoxy had rebuilt Protestant teaching with scholastic tools, while Catholic reform at Trent drew on Aquinas.
Practical divinity and the religion of the heart

English Puritans such as William Perkins defined theology as the science of living blessedly; German Pietists led by Spener and Francke called for new birth, Bible study and practical love. Both shaped evangelical Christianity.
Reason on the throne

The Enlightenment made reason the judge of revelation; Deists reduced Christianity to natural religion and Kant to morality. Schleiermacher responded by grounding theology in religious experience, and the liberal Protestantism of Ritschl and Harnack followed.
Barth and the 20th-century revolts

After 1914 Karl Barth broke with liberalism to proclaim God’s self-revelation; Bultmann and Tillich took an existentialist path; exiled Orthodox theologians called for a neo-patristic synthesis; French Catholics returned to the Fathers and were vindicated at Vatican II, ending the reign of the neo-Thomist manuals launched by Aeterni Patris (1879).
Theology from below

From the late 1960s, liberation theology in Latin America, Black theology in the USA and South Africa, and feminist and womanist theology argued that the experience of the poor and oppressed must shape theological method. Critics feared politics would override the gospel; supporters replied that all theology is contextual.
Many tongues: theology in world Christianity

Postliberals and Radical Orthodoxy challenged neutral foundations, while the centre of Christianity moved south. African, Asian and Pentecostal theologians now argue that the gospel must be thought in every language and culture, as Pentecost itself suggests.
paths/the-great-schools-of-theology/quiz: Which school favoured the historical-grammatical sense of Scripture over allegory?
Diodore, Theodore of Mopsuestia and John Chrysostom represent the Antiochene emphasis on history and grammar.
Who wrote "I believe in order to understand" in the Proslogion?
Anselm of Canterbury, Proslogion 1 (1078), echoing Augustine.
Which book became the standard theology textbook of the medieval universities?
Lombard’s Four Books of Sentences was commented on by every medieval master, including Aquinas and Luther.
What did Leo XIII’s Aeterni Patris (1879) promote?
It made Thomism the norm for Catholic philosophy and seminary teaching.
Whose theology grounded doctrine in the "feeling of absolute dependence"?
Schleiermacher, the father of liberal Protestant theology.
Which movement did Georges Florovsky call for in 1936?
Florovsky urged Orthodox theologians to acquire the "mind of the Fathers".
Which theologian founded Black theology with Black Theology and Black Power (1969)?
James H. Cone, of Union Theological Seminary, New York.
